explain.say: How long do you think it takes to judge a stranger's face? A minute? Ten seconds? Scientists found it takes about one tenth of a second! Look at the board. It asks why first impressions stick. Let us look at the reasons together.

explain.say: See the first reason, fast judging? Your brain makes snap guesses about whether someone seems friendly or trustworthy, just from their face, before they even speak. These guesses are quick but often wrong. Have you ever been wrong about someone at first?

explain.say: Now look at first info wins. Information that comes first colours how we see everything after it. Psychologists call this the primacy effect. If a new classmate seems rude on day one, you might read later kind acts as fake. Can you think of an example?

faq.a: A first impression is the quick opinion we form about someone when we first meet them, often from their face, clothes, voice or a few words.

faq.q: How fast do we judge people?
faq.a: Very fast. In a 2006 Princeton study, people formed judgements about trustworthiness from a face shown for just one tenth of a second, and longer looks barely changed them.
asks: Can you judge someone in seconds?

faq.a: The primacy effect means information we get first has a stronger effect on our opinion than information that comes later. First words and actions colour everything after.
asks: Tell me about first info wins
Why does first information matter more?

faq.a: The halo effect is when one good trait, like being attractive or friendly, makes us assume a person has other good traits too, like being clever or kind. Psychologist Edward Thorndike named it in 1920.

faq.q: Can you change a first impression?
faq.a: Yes, but it takes more time and evidence than forming it. Spending real time with someone and noticing what does not fit your first guess helps you see the real person.
asks: How do I fix a bad first impression?

facts: Willis and Todorov (2006) found people judged trustworthiness from faces shown for 100 milliseconds, about one tenth of a second.
Edward Thorndike described the halo effect in 1920 after noticing that officers rated soldiers good or bad across all qualities at once.

quiz.why: One good trait spreading to others in our minds is the halo effect.

quiz.say: About how long does it take to form a first judgement of a face?
quiz.why: Studies show we form snap judgements in about 100 milliseconds.

wrong.1: It happens far faster than a minute.
wrong.2: Snap judgements happen almost instantly, not over days.
